# Approximation Methods - 1

In this chapter we shall consider the time-independent perturbation theory.
That is, the Hamiltonian of the system is written as 
$$
H = H_0 + \lambda H^\op,
$$ {#eq-app1}
where $H_0$ is a Hamiltonian simple enough to be solved exactly and $H^\op$
is a perturbation to it. The parameter $\lambda$ varies from $0$ to $1$ and
determines the "strength" of the perturbation.

Since the system with $\lambda = 0$ is solvable exactly, we know the eigenvalues
and eigenstates of
$$
H_0\ket{n^0} = E_n^0\ket{n^0}.
$$ {#eq-app2}
Our aim is solve
$$
H\ket{n} = E_n\ket{n},
$$ {#eq-app3}
using the solution of @eq-app2. The portion $\lambda H^\op$ is a perturbation,
that is, its impact on the system is small as compared to that of $H_0$. We,
therefore, expect that the eigenvalues and eigenstates of $H$ will not be 
drastically different from those of $H_0$. The procedure to build them depends
on whether the spectrum of $H_0$ is degenerate or not. We will first consider
the simpler case of the non-degenerate spectrum.

## Non-degenerate spectrum
We assume that we can express $\ket{n}$ and $E_n$ as power series of the form
$$
\begin{eqnarray}
E_n &=& E_n^0 + \lambda E_n^1 + \lambda^2 E_n^2 + \cdots \\
\ket{n} &=& \ket{n^0} + \lambda\ket{n^1} + \lambda^2\ket{n^2} + \cdots
\end{eqnarray}
$$ {#eq-app4}
Substituting these forms in @eq-app3, taking into account @eq-app1 and
@eq-app3 and equating the powers of $\lambda$ on either sides of the equation
we get 
$$
\begin{eqnarray}
H_0\ket{n^0} &=& E_n^0\ket{n^0} \\
H_0\ket{n^1} + H^\op\ket{n^0} &=& E_n^0\ket{n^1} + E_n^1\ket{n^0} \\
H_0\ket{n^2} + H^\op\ket{n^1} &=& E_n^2\ket{n^0} + E_n^1\ket{n^1} + 
E_n^0\ket{n^2} \\
H_0\ket{n^3} + H^\op\ket{n^2} &=& E_n^3\ket{n^0} + E_n^2\ket{n^1} + 
E_n^1\ket{n^2} + E_n^0\ket{n^3} \\
\vdots &=& \vdots
\end{eqnarray}
$$ {#eq-app5}
Since $H_0$ is hermitian, multiplying the second of the above equation by 
$\bra{n^0}$ gives,
$$
E_n^1 = \braket{n^0|H^\op|n^0}.
$$ {#eq-app6}
This is the first order correction to the energy eigenvalue $E_n^0$. Likewise,
the second order correction is
$$
E_n^2 = \braket{n^0|H^\op - E_n^1|n^1}
$$ {#eq-app7}
and the third order correction is
$$
E_n^3 = \braket{n^0|H^\op - E_n^1|n^2} - 2E_n^2\braket{n^0|n^1}.
$$ {#eq-app8}

We now proceed to find the eigenstates. The first order correction in @eq-app6
depends on the unperturbed eigenstates and the pertubation. However, the second
order correction needs perturbed eigenstates. We assume that the problem for
$H_0$ is completely solved, that is, we know its eigenvalues and eigenstates. 
We assume that $\ket{n^1}$ belongs to linear space spanned by the eigenstates of
the unperturbed operator. Therefore, we express it as
$$
\ket{n^1} = \sum_{m \ge 1}a_m^1\ket{m^0}.
$$ {#eq-app9}
Substituting this in the second of equations @eq-app5 we get
$$
a_k^1 = \frac{\braket{k^0|H^\op|n^0}}{E_k^0 - E_n^0}, \text{ if } k \ne n
$$ {#eq-app10}
and $E_n^1 = \braket{n^0|H^\op|n^0}$ if $k = n$. The second equation is
identical to @eq-app6. The coefficient $a_n^1$ is undertermined and is set to 
zero. Thus, from @eq-app9,
$$
\ket{n^1} = \sum_{m \ne n}\frac{\braket{k^0|H^\op|n^0}}{E_k^0 - E_n^0}\ket{m^0}
$$
so that from @eq-app7,
$$
E_n^2 = \sum_{m \ne n}\frac{|\braket{m^0|H^\op|n^0}|^2}{E_n^0 - E_m^0}.
$$ {#eq-app11}

## Degenerate spectrum
We now consider the situation in which the unperturbed state with eigenvalue 
$E_k^0$ is degenerate and has multiple eigenstates $\ket{\psi_{k, 1}^0}, \ldots,
\ket{\psi_{k, r}^0}$. We continue with the perturbed Hamiltonian of the form 
$H = H_0 + \lambda H^\op$, with $\lambda \in [0, 1]$. If $H\ket{\psi} = 
E\ket{\psi}$ is such that $E \rightarrow E_k^0$ when $\lambda \rightarrow 0$ 
then we cannot infer to which $\ket{\psi_{k, i}^0}$ does $\ket{\psi}$ tend to 
because there are multiple options. The set $\{\ket{\psi_{k,i}^0} : i = 1, 
\ldots, r\}$ is a subspace of the Hilbert space of the eigenstates of $H_0$ and 
we can always assume it to be orthonormal. Thus,
$$
\braket{\psi_{kr}^0|\psi_{ks}^0} = \delta_{rs}.
$$ {#eq-app12}
When $\lambda \ne 0$, it is quite possible that the degeneracy is lost and we 
have
$$
H\ket{\psi_{kr}} = E_{kr}\ket{\psi_{kr}}
$$ {#eq-app13}
where $E_{kr} \rightarrow E_k^0$ as $\lambda \rightarrow 0$. We now express
$$
\ket{\psi_{kr}} = \ket{\chi^0_{kr}} + \lambda\ket{\psi^1_{kr}} + \lambda^2
\ket{\psi^2_{kr}} + \ldots
$$ {#eq-app14}
where $\ket{\chi^0_{kr}}$ is the eigenstate to which $\ket{\psi_{kr}}$ tends to
as the perturbation is turned off. It is labelled differently because we do not
know to which of the unpertubed eigenstates $\ket{\psi_{kr}}$ will tend to as
$\lambda \rightarrow 0$. However, we do know that $\ket{\chi^0_{kr}}$ must have
eigenvalue $E_k^0$. Therefore, it must belong to the subspace spanned by the
eigenstates belonging to $E_k^0$ so that
$$
\ket{\chi_{kr}^0} = \sum_{s=1}^Nc_{rs}\ket{\psi_{ks}^0},
$$ {#eq-app15}
where we assumed that $E_k^0$ is $N$-fold degenerate. As in the degenerate case,
assume that 
$$
E_{kr} = \sum_{n \ge 0}\lambda^n E_{kr}^n,
$$ {#eq-app16}
where $E_{kr}^0 = E_k^0$ because of degeneracy. Substuting @eq-app14 and 
@eq-app16 in @eq-app13 we get for $\lambda = 0$, the expected equation
$$
H_0\ket{\chi^0_{kr}} = E_k^0\ket{\chi^0_{kr}}
$$ {#eq-app17}
and
$$
H_0\ket{\psi^1_{kr}} + H^\op\ket{\chi^0_{kr}} = E^0_k\ket{\psi^1_{kr}} +
E^1_k\ket{\chi^0_{kr}}
$$ {#eq-app18}
as the correction first order in $\lambda$. We now use, @eq-app15 in it to get
$$
H_0\ket{\psi^1_{kr}} + \sum_{s=1}^Nc_{rs}H^\op\ket{\psi_{kr}^0} = 
E^0_k\ket{\psi^1_{kr}} + E^1_k\sum_{s=1}^Nc_{rs}\ket{\psi_{ks}^0}.
$$ {#eq-app19}
As we did in the non-degenerate case in @eq-app9, we write
$$
\ket{\psi^1_{kr}} = \sum_{ms}a^1_{kr,ms}\ket{\psi^0_{ms}},
$$ {#eq-app20}
where $\{\ket{\psi^0_{ms}}\}$ is the complete set of eigenstates of $H_0$, so 
that @eq-app19 becomes
$$
\sum_{ms}a^1_{kr,ms}H_0\ket{\psi^0_{ms}} + 
\sum_{s=1}^Nc_{rs}H^\op\ket{\psi_{kr}^0} = 
E^0_k\sum_{ms}a^1_{kr,ms}\ket{\psi^0_{ms}} + 
E^1_k\sum_{s=1}^Nc_{rs}\ket{\psi_{ks}^0}.
$$ {#eq-app21}
Since $H_0\ket{\psi_{ms}^0}=E_m^0\ket{\psi_{ms}^0}$, we have, after rearranging 
terms,
$$
\sum_{ms}a^1_{kr,ms}\left(E^0_{m} - E_k^0\right)\ket{\psi^0_{ms}} + 
(H^\op - E^1_k )\sum_{s=1}^Nc_{rs}\ket{\psi_{ks}^0}.
$$ {#eq-app22}
Taking an inner product with $\ket{\psi_{ku}^0}$, the first term vanishes and the
second one gives
$$
\sum_{s=1}^N c_{rs}\left(\braket{\psi_{ku}^0|H^\op|\psi_{ks}^0} - E_k^1 
\delta_{us}\right) = 0.
$$ {#eq-app23}
These are $N$ linear equations in $c_{rs}$. They have unique, non-trivial 
solutions only if
$$
\det{\braket{\psi_{ku}^0|H^\op|\psi_{ks}^0} - E_k^1\delta_{us}} = 0.
$$ {#eq-app24}
The roots of this equation give the first order corrections $E_{k1}^1, \ldots
E_{kN}^1$ to the eigenvalues. If they are all different, the perturbation has
split the originally degenerate state into $N$ non-degenerate ones. If some
roots are equal then we look at the second order corrections to remove 
additional degeneracy. We continue this way until the degeneracy is completely
removed. The degeneracy may never be removed if $H_0$ and $H$ have similar
symmetry.
